doc.title: Geometric Deep Learning Grids, Groups, Graphs, Geodesics, and Gauges

proposal.title: Geometric Deep Learning Grids, Groups, Graphs, Geodesics, and Gauges
proposal.gist: Deep learning architectures for grids, graphs, groups, geodesics and gauges all derive from one blueprint: respecting the symmetries and invariances of the data's domain.
proposal.question: Geometric Deep Learning — how can symmetry and invariance unify the design of neural network architectures? (a blueprint with five domains and example models)

children.title: Preface
children.gist: Following Felix Klein's Erlangen Programme, which unified geometries by their symmetry groups, this text seeks to unify deep learning architectures through the same principle of invariance.
children.question: Geometric unification — can deep learning's many architectures be organized the way Klein organized geometry? (a historical analogy)

children.title: Notation
children.gist: A reference table of mathematical symbols used throughout, covering domains, signals, groups, operators and geometric quantities.

children.title: Introduction
children.gist: Deep learning succeeds on high-dimensional tasks because real-world data carries geometric regularities, and exposing these through symmetry principles can unify architectures like CNNs, GNNs and Transformers under one framework.
children.question: Geometric regularity — why do symmetry principles unify seemingly different neural network architectures? (a programmatic argument)

children.title: Learning in High Dimensions
children.gist: Learning a generic function in high dimensions needs exponentially many samples, so successful learning must encode regularity assumptions, yet the usual regularity classes (Lipschitz, Sobolev, low-dimensional projections) all fail to escape this curse realistically.
children.question: Curse of dimensionality — why do standard notions of function regularity fail to make high-dimensional learning tractable? (a statistical argument)

children.title: Supervised Learning Setup
children.gist: Supervised learning draws samples from a high-dimensional data distribution and seeks a function matching labels, measured by expected loss on new data, requiring regularity assumptions to succeed.

children.title: Inductive Bias via Function Regularity
children.gist: Neural networks can approximate almost any function, so genuine inductive bias instead comes from preferring the simplest fitting function under some complexity measure, as in splines or weight norms.

children.title: The Curse of Dimensionality
children.gist: Standard regularity classes like Lipschitz or Sobolev functions require exponentially many samples as dimension grows, and even sparsity-based neural network priors only escape this by assuming unrealistic low-dimensional structure in the target function.

children.title: Geometric Priors
children.gist: Because the physical world's data lives on structured domains, exploiting the domain's symmetry and its ability to be coarsened at multiple scales (two complementary priors) yields deep learning blueprints like CNNs that beat the curse of dimensionality.
children.question: Geometric priors — how do symmetry and scale separation together let deep networks escape the curse of dimensionality? (two principles, with examples)

children.title: Signals, domains, and geometric priors
children.gist: Machine learning systems operate on signals living in a vector space over some domain, and physically structured data gains two exploitable priors, symmetry and scale separation, which let architectures like CNNs escape the curse of dimensionality despite the impossibility proofs of the previous section.

children.title: Symmetries, Representations, and Invariance
children.gist: Symmetries of a domain form a mathematical group, whose actions on points extend to linear representations acting on signals, letting functions be classified as invariant (unaffected by the symmetry) or equivariant (transformed consistently with it).

children.title: Isomorphisms and Automorphisms
children.gist: Different levels of structure on a domain, from bare sets up to differentiable manifolds, yield different symmetry groups as subgroups of larger ones, and this distinction separates automorphisms, which map an object to itself, from isomorphisms, which equate two distinct but structurally identical objects such as graphs.

children.title: Deformation Stability
children.gist: Because real-world transformations are rarely exact symmetries, functions can instead be required to be approximately stable, with their output changing by an amount bounded by a complexity measure of how far a deformation is from the true symmetry group, for both signal deformations and deformations of the domain itself.

children.title: Scale Separation
children.gist: Because global Fourier representations are unstable under small deformations, whereas localized multiscale wavelet-like decompositions remain stable, functions that factor through a hierarchy of coarsened domains can separate local from long-range interactions and thereby beat the curse of dimensionality.

children.title: The Blueprint of Geometric Deep Learning
children.gist: Combining symmetry, stability and scale separation yields a universal blueprint built from four blocks, local equivariant layers, nonlinearities, local pooling and global invariant pooling, composed to construct any function respecting the domain's symmetry group, instantiated differently across CNNs, GNNs and Transformers.
children.sourceHeading: 3.5 The Blueprint of Geometric Deep Learning

children.title: Geometric Domains: the 5 Gs
children.gist: Grids, groups, graphs, geodesics and gauges are the five geometric domains whose underlying symmetry structures, from global transformation groups down to local reference frames, give rise to the specific forms that convolution, equivariance and invariance take in each setting.
children.question: The 5 Gs — what distinguishes the symmetry structure of each geometric domain, and how does it shape convolution-like operations on it? (five domains surveyed in turn)

children.title: The Five Geometric Domains
children.gist: Grids, groups, graphs, geodesics and gauges are the five geometric domains this text treats, ordered not by generality but to highlight the shared and distinguishing symmetry concepts underlying the Geometric Deep Learning blueprint.

children.title: Graphs and Sets
children.gist: Graphs model relations between unordered nodes, so valid functions on them must be permutation invariant or equivariant, and a local neighbourhood-aggregation recipe built from an invariant function gives a general way to construct such equivariant functions.

children.title: Grids and Euclidean spaces
children.gist: Grids are graphs with fixed node order, so translation invariance replaces permutation invariance, and this symmetry alone forces linear equivariant maps to be convolutions, whose Fourier-diagonalisation explains why frequency-domain filtering works and extends toward graphs and continuous signals.

children.title: Groups and Homogeneous spaces
children.gist: Replacing the translation group with any locally compact symmetry group yields a general group convolution that is provably equivariant, illustrated on cyclic shifts and spherical rotations, though convolution stays practical only on low-dimensional domains and relies on the domain being a homogeneous space where every point looks alike.

children.title: Geodesics and Manifolds
children.gist: Manifolds generally lack a global symmetry group, so instead of sliding filters researchers exploit intrinsic structure—Riemannian metrics, parallel transport, geodesic distances and isometries—to build Laplacian-based spectral and tangent-space spatial convolutions that stay invariant to deformation yet depend on an arbitrarily chosen local frame or gauge.

children.title: Gauges and Bundles
children.gist: Generalising the tangent frame to any vector bundle introduces gauge symmetry, where changing the local frame must transform feature representations by a structure-group element, and functions are gauge equivariant only when filters commute with that group action after parallel transport.

children.title: Geometric graphs and Meshes
children.gist: Triangular meshes sit between graphs and manifolds, carrying an intrinsic cotangent Laplacian whose eigenbasis gives isometry-invariant spectral convolution, while the functional-maps view treats meshes as operators and yields remeshing-invariant functions depending only on an operator's spectrum.

children.title: Geometric Deep Learning Models
children.gist: Enforcing the blueprint's prescriptions on different domains and groups recovers nearly all popular deep learning architectures, from CNNs and GNNs to Transformers, equivariant message-passing networks, intrinsic mesh CNNs, and gated RNNs like the LSTM.
children.question: Geometric Deep Learning Models — how does one blueprint, applied across domains, give rise to CNNs, GNNs, Transformers, and gated RNNs alike? (eight architecture families)

children.title: Chapter Overview
children.gist: This chapter shows that enforcing the Geometric Deep Learning blueprint on each domain and symmetry group recovers CNNs, group-equivariant CNNs, GNNs, Transformers, equivariant message-passing networks, mesh CNNs and gated RNNs like the LSTM.

children.title: Convolutional Neural Networks
children.gist: CNNs implement the blueprint's translation-equivariant local linear operator as ordinary convolution, which composes with nonlinearities, multiscale coarsening, residual reparametrisation, normalisation and data augmentation into the standard architecture.

children.title: Group-equivariant CNNs
children.gist: Generalising convolution to any homogeneous space by moving a filter via the group action yields group-equivariant CNNs, demonstrated on discrete rotation groups for 3D medical images, DNA reverse-complement symmetry, and spherical CNNs computed efficiently via Fourier methods.

children.title: Graph Neural Networks
children.gist: GNNs realise the blueprint on graphs using permutation symmetry, and nearly all GNN layers in the literature reduce to three flavours—convolutional, attentional, and message-passing—that trade expressiveness for scalability and ease of training.

children.title: Deep Sets, Transformers, Latent Graph Inference
children.gist: Treating unordered sets as graphs with no, complete, or inferred edges recovers Deep Sets from an empty adjacency, Transformers' self-attention from a complete graph with positional encodings, and the open problem of learning a latent adjacency matrix directly from data.
children.sourceHeading: 5.4 Deep Sets, Transformers, and Latent Graph Inference

children.title: Equivariant Message Passing Networks
children.gist: When graph nodes carry spatial coordinates, as in molecules, message-passing layers can be made equivariant to rigid Euclidean motions by routing all coordinate dependence through pairwise distances, with richer irreducible- and regular-representation approaches extending beyond scalar features.

children.title: Intrinsic Mesh CNNs
children.gist: Mesh CNNs discretise convolution using geodesic polar patches around each point, resolving the ambiguous choice of local reference direction (the gauge) through isotropic filters, fixed gauges, angular max pooling, or fully gauge-equivariant filters that transport features consistently between neighbours.

children.title: Recurrent Neural Networks
children.gist: Sequential data processed step-by-step by RNNs can be shown to exhibit translation equivariance over time once sequences are suitably zero-padded, though plain SimpleRNNs still suffer from vanishing or exploding gradients during long-sequence training.

children.title: Long Short-Term Memory Networks
children.gist: The LSTM adds a gated memory cell whose input, forget and output gates are learned from data to control information flow, and this gating mechanism provably makes gated RNNs invariant to time-warping transformations, explaining their strength at long-range dependencies, as used in sequence-to-sequence translation and attention models.

children.title: Problems and Applications
children.gist: The five geometric domains and their symmetry-respecting architectures already drive real breakthroughs across chemistry, biology, recommendation, traffic, vision, games, language, medicine, and physics.
children.question: Applications — where has Geometric Deep Learning already produced concrete, high-impact real-world results? (a survey across a dozen fields)

children.title: Overview of applications
children.gist: Geometric regularities pervade real-world data, so many of the most influential 21st-century machine learning successes are instances of Geometric Deep Learning, often unrecognized as such, which this chapter surveys non-exhaustively.

children.title: Chemistry and Drug Design
children.gist: Because synthesizable molecule space is vast (around 10^60), graph neural networks now screen candidate drugs computationally, as shown when one model discovered the antibiotic Halicin among molecules originally meant for diabetes.

children.title: Drug Repositioning
children.gist: Repurposing already-approved drugs is cheaper than inventing new ones, and graph-based 'network medicine' models drug and biomolecule interactions to predict side effects, combination therapies, and even food-derived drug-like compounds.

children.title: Protein biology
children.gist: Since a protein's 3D fold determines its function and drug interactions, graph and mesh neural networks like AlphaFold-adjacent methods and MaSIF now predict structure, function, and even design novel cancer immunotherapy proteins.

children.title: Recommender Systems and Social Networks
children.gist: Graph representation learning, pioneered at scale by Pinterest's PinSage and used by Alibaba and Amazon, powers recommendation via link prediction, and also underlies Fabula AI's misinformation-detection system later acquired by Twitter.

children.title: Traffic forecasting
children.gist: Modeling road networks as graphs lets graph neural networks predict estimated time of arrival for routes, a technique now deployed in production by Google Maps and Baidu Maps worldwide.

children.title: Object recognition
children.gist: The ImageNet challenge drove convolutional networks like AlexNet, VGG-16, and ResNets to surpass human-level image classification, with their design tricks also enabling fine-grained object detection and segmentation tasks.

children.title: Game playing
children.gist: Convolutional networks serve as feature extractors in reinforcement learning, as in DeepMind's AlphaGo and its successors AlphaZero and MuZero, and in Agent57 which first matched human performance across all 57 Atari games.

children.title: Text and speech synthesis
children.gist: On one-dimensional grids of text and speech, dilated convolutions like WaveNet and then Transformer models like BERT and GPT-3 replaced recurrent networks, enabling human-like speech synthesis and large-scale text generation.

children.title: Healthcare
children.gist: Geometric Deep Learning aids medicine through grid-based scan diagnosis, mesh models of organs and brain surfaces, functional brain networks for neuropathology, and patient-similarity graphs built from demographic or health-record data.

children.title: Particle physics and astrophysics
children.gist: Particle physicists adopted graph neural networks to classify particle jets and detect astrophysical neutrinos, while equivariant networks respecting physical symmetries like the Lorentz group now analyze cosmic radio and microwave data.

children.title: Virtual and Augmented Reality
children.gist: Mesh convolutional networks, developed for motion capture correspondence and 3D shape synthesis of bodies and faces, now power real-time hand-pose estimation deployed in Snap's augmented reality products.

children.title: Historic Perspective
children.gist: Symmetry has organized mathematics, physics and machine learning for over a century, and tracing that lineage shows Geometric Deep Learning as a natural culmination rather than an invention, consolidating decades of parallel independent discoveries.
children.question: Historic Perspective — how did symmetry's long history in mathematics and physics converge, through many independent lines, into today's Geometric Deep Learning? (a historical survey)

children.title: Symmetry Through History
children.gist: Hermann Weyl's reflections on symmetry trace the idea from Sumerian design and Pythagorean geometry through Plato's five solids to Kepler's explanation of snowflakes' six-fold structure via particle packing.

children.title: Symmetry in Mathematics and Physics
children.gist: Group theory, developed by Galois, Lie, Klein and Cartan, became mathematics' language for symmetry, while Noether showed every physical symmetry yields a conservation law, and gauge invariance later unified electromagnetism and the other forces in the Standard Model.

children.title: Early Use of Symmetry in Machine Learning
children.gist: Symmetry entered pattern recognition early through equivariant feature detectors and the Group Invariance Theorem for Perceptrons, culminating in Fukushima's shift-invariant Neocognitron and LeCun's convolutional neural networks inspired by the visual cortex.
children.sourceHeading: Early Use of Symmetry in Machine Learning

children.title: Graph Neural Networks
children.gist: Graph neural networks trace back to 1990s work on tree and structure processing, with the term itself coined after 2000 by Gori and Scarselli using recurrent fixed-point computation, later replaced by the gated GNN model borrowing RNN gating mechanisms.

children.title: Computational Chemistry
children.gist: Independently of mainstream GNN research, computational chemistry drove graph-based molecular modelling from the 1990s onward, producing techniques like molecular fingerprinting and quantum-property prediction that today underpin drug-screening successes such as new antibiotics.

children.title: Node Embeddings
children.gist: Early unsupervised graph representation learning relied on random-walk embeddings like DeepWalk and node2vec, later shown equivalent to matrix factorisation, before the field shifted toward contrastive, mutual-information-based methods such as Deep Graph Infomax.

children.title: Probabilistic Graphical Models
children.gist: Graph neural networks also arose from probabilistic graphical models, where nodes represent random variables and message passing supports inference, a link formalised by structure2vec and later extended to conditional random fields and Markov logic networks.

children.title: The Weisfeiler-Lehman Formalism
children.gist: The Weisfeiler-Lehman graph isomorphism test sets a provable ceiling on what ordinary GNNs can distinguish, motivating injective aggregation functions like summation and architectures such as GIN and PNA that approach or match this limit.

children.title: Higher-order Methods
children.gist: Because real molecules and graphs often carry rich enough features to work despite WL limits, researchers built higher-order k-GNNs, invariant graph networks over tuples, and structural augmentations like identifiers and motif-level modelling to exceed WL's expressive power.

children.title: Signal Processing and Harmonic Analysis
children.gist: Researchers explained convolutional networks' success using harmonic analysis tools such as Poggio's M-theory templates, Simoncelli's steerable pyramids for texture generation, and Mallat's scattering transforms built from fixed wavelet decompositions instead of learned filters.

children.title: Signal Processing on Graphs and Meshes
children.gist: Spectral graph neural networks grew from graph Fourier transforms and graph signal processing in the 2000s–2010s, while non-Euclidean harmonic analysis on meshes, predating this by a decade, produced shape descriptors and functional maps still used in computer graphics.
children.sourceHeading: Signal Processing on Graph and Meshes

children.title: Computer Graphics and Geometry Processing
children.gist: Intrinsic shape-analysis methods in computer graphics led to Geodesic CNNs, MoNet and graph attention networks, alongside independently developed point-cloud models like PointNet and DGCNN that pioneered learning the graph structure itself, as later exploited by Transformers.

children.title: Algorithmic Reasoning
children.gist: Beyond spatial domains, invariances also arise from computation itself, inspiring neural architectures that mimic algorithms' preconditions and postconditions, with GNNs shown to align with dynamic programming and extended to simulations and extrapolation studies.

children.title: Naming Geometric Deep Learning
children.gist: The term Geometric Deep Learning originated in a 2015 ERC grant and a 2017 IEEE paper announcing a new field, and the book's '5 Gs' framework—grids, graphs, groups, gauges, and the authors' added geodesics—names its organising structures.
